chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, from Ismail ibn al-Fadl al-Hashimi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who leased from the Sultan (ruling authority) from the government land (ard al-kharaj) for a specified amount of Dirhams, or for a specified amount of foodstuff. Then he sub-leased it and stipulated upon the one who cultivated it that he would distribute half, or less than that or more, and for him in the land after that would be the excess. Is that correct for him? He said: Yes, when he digs out a river for them or does some work for them to assist them with that, so that would be for him.

He said: And I asked him about the man who leases a land from the government land for a specified amount of Dirhams, or with a known amount of foodstuff, so he sub-leases it piece by piece, or a Jareyba by a Jareyba, with a specified thing. So there happened to be some excess for him regarding what he had leased from the Sultan, and he had not spent anything upon it. Or he leases out that land in pieces upon a stipulation that he would give them the seeds and the expenditure. So there happens to be some excess for him regarding that, upon his lessees, and would there be for him the fertility of the land or would it not be for him? He said: Whenever you lease a land, so you spend something therein, or do some repair work in it, so there is no problem with what you have mentioned.

key_terms.يُقَاسِمَهُ: He would share the crop with him

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for a person to profit from sub-leasing government land in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi establishes the permissibility of sub-leasing (ijarah) with profit retention, a foundational principle for agricultural tenancy in Shia jurisprudence. It distinguishes between mere speculation and legitimate investment by requiring the lessee to contribute labor or capital, such as digging canals or providing seeds, thereby linking ownership of the 'fruit' to the effort of cultivation. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on fairness in contracts, ensuring that the lessor benefits from their asset while the cultivator is rewarded for their direct input.
